title: AIX: SMIT + LPAR management fundamentals
excerpt: Administración de AIX con SMIT + gestión de LPARs desde HMC.
body:
## AIX overview
IBM Unix corriendo en Power hardware:
- POWER7/8/9/10
- Multi-tenant vía LPARs (Logical Partitions)
- HMC (Hardware Management Console) para managing

## SMIT (System Management Interface Tool)
Interfaz menú-driven para admin tasks. Alternativo a memorizar comandos.

### Modes
```bash
smit           # ASCII menu (default)
smit -C        # curses interface
smitty         # simplified ASCII (más usado)
```

### Navigation
- F3 = back
- F4 = list values disponibles
- F6 = command (muestra el comando que se ejecutaría)
- F10 = exit
- Esc + 6 = command en terminals sin function keys

### Common tasks
- `smitty user` — user management
- `smitty group` — groups
- `smitty fs` — filesystems
- `smitty tcpip` — network
- `smitty install` — software
- `smitty jfs2` — JFS2 filesystems

### SMIT logs
Cada session logs a:
- `~/smit.log` — actions performed
- `~/smit.script` — commands ejecutados (útil para scripts posteriores)

## LPAR (Logical Partition)
Slice del physical hardware:
- CPU (dedicated o shared processor pools)
- Memory
- Storage (via VIOS)
- Network (via VIOS SEA)

### Tipos
- **Dedicated** — CPUs asignadas exclusivamente
- **Shared** — micropartitioning (fracciones de CPU, 0.1 hasta N)

### VIOS (Virtual I/O Server)
Special LPAR que provides virtualized I/O a otras LPARs:
- Virtual SCSI (storage)
- Virtual FC (Fibre Channel NPIV)
- SEA (Shared Ethernet Adapter — network)

## HMC (Hardware Management Console)
Appliance (physical o virtual) que manages Power servers:
- Create/modify LPARs
- Start/stop LPARs
- Firmware updates
- Console access
- Performance monitoring

### Acceso
- Web browser: `https://hmc-ip`
- SSH: `ssh hscroot@hmc-ip`

### CLI
```bash
# Ver managed systems
lssyscfg -r sys

# Ver LPARs de un system
lssyscfg -r lpar -m <system-name>

# Ver estado LPAR
lssyscfg -r lpar -m System1 --filter 'lpar_names=aix01' -F name,state

# Ver CPU + memory
lshwres -m System1 -r proc --level lpar
lshwres -m System1 -r mem --level lpar

# Start LPAR
chsysstate -m System1 -r lpar -o on -n aix01 -f normal

# Shutdown LPAR (graceful)
chsysstate -m System1 -r lpar -o osshutdown -n aix01

# Force off
chsysstate -m System1 -r lpar -o shutdown -n aix01 --immed
```

## Console access
```bash
# Desde HMC
vtmenu
# menu de LPARs → seleccionar → open console

# Console via CLI
mkvterm -m System1 -p aix01
# ~. para exit
```

## AIX básico commands

### System info
```bash
oslevel                    # OS version
oslevel -s                 # SP level (con TL + SP)
prtconf                    # hardware summary (extenso)
uname -a                   # kernel version
lparstat                   # LPAR utilization
vmstat                     # memory + CPU
iostat                     # disk I/O
topas                      # like `top` — real-time dashboard
```

### User management
```bash
# Create user
mkuser -a home=/home/juan groups=staff juan

# Change password
passwd juan

# List users
lsuser ALL
lsuser juan                # single user

# Modify
chuser groups=staff,sap juan

# Delete
rmuser juan               # keeps home dir
rmuser -p juan            # removes home dir + entries en other files
```

### Groups
```bash
mkgroup sap
lsgroup ALL
chgroup users=juan,pedro,maria sap
rmgroup sap
```

## AIX passwd rules
En `/etc/security/user`:
```
minlen = 8
minother = 1              # min special/digit
maxrepeats = 2
minage = 0                # weeks (0 = no min)
maxage = 13               # weeks (~90 days)
histsize = 5
```

## Boot process
1. Firmware POST
2. NVRAM loads bootlist
3. Boot device (usually hdisk0)
4. `/sbin/init` starts
5. `/etc/inittab` runs
6. Runlevel 2 (multi-user)

### Boot management
```bash
# Ver bootlist
bootlist -m normal -o

# Change bootlist
bootlist -m normal hdisk0 hdisk1 cd0

# Recovery boot
bootlist -m service cd0
```

## errpt (Error Report)
AIX centralized error log:

```bash
errpt                     # summary — most recent first
errpt -a                  # detailed
errpt -j <error-id>       # specific error detail
errpt -d H                # only hardware errors
errpt -d S                # only software errors
errpt -s 0801000024       # since date (MMDDhhmmYY)

# Cleanup
errclear 30               # remove errors older than 30 days
```

### Common errpt entries
- `EPOW_SUS_CHRP` — power supply issue
- `SC_DISK_ERR3` — disk error
- `TS_LOGREFUSED_ER` — TCP connection refused pattern
- `SPD_INF` — SP (Service Processor) info

## Subsystems (SRC — System Resource Controller)
AIX equivalent to systemd:

```bash
lssrc -a                        # all subsystems
lssrc -s inetd                  # specific subsystem
lssrc -g tcpip                  # group

startsrc -s inetd
stopsrc -s inetd
refresh -s inetd                # reload config
```

## Filesystems
### View
```bash
df -g                    # in GB
df -k                    # in KB
lsfs                     # all filesystems configured
lsvg                     # volume groups
lspv                     # physical volumes
lslv                     # logical volumes
```

### Structure (LVM)
- **Physical Volume (PV)** — disk (hdiskN)
- **Volume Group (VG)** — logical container of PVs (rootvg, datavg)
- **Logical Volume (LV)** — slice of VG
- **Filesystem (FS)** — formatted LV

### Extend filesystem
```bash
chfs -a size=+1G /home
# o smitty chfs
```

Dynamic, no unmount required (JFS2).

## Networking
```bash
# Interfaces
netstat -in
ifconfig -a

# Config interface
chdev -l en0 -a netaddr=10.0.0.10 -a netmask=255.255.255.0 -a state=up

# Add default route
route add default 10.0.0.1

# Persistent (in ODM)
chdev -l inet0 -a route=net,-hopcount,0,,0,10.0.0.1
```

## Software (bffs — Backup File Format)

### Ver installed
```bash
lslpp -l                       # all filesets
lslpp -l bos.rte               # specific
instfix -i -k 'IY12345'        # by APAR/fix number
instfix -i | grep -i sap       # search
```

### Install
```bash
inutoc /path/to/media          # generate TOC
installp -a -d /path -X <package>
# Or smitty install_all
```

### Reject / commit
```bash
installp -r <package>          # reject (uninstall applied but not committed)
installp -c <package>          # commit (final)
```

## Best practices

### 1. TL + SP kept current
AIX Technology Levels (TL) + Service Packs (SP). Apply annually at least.

### 2. errpt review daily
Automate:
```bash
0 6 * * * root /usr/bin/errpt -s $(date +'%m%d000000%y' --date='yesterday') | mail admin@empresa.com
```

### 3. VG naming
Separate rootvg from data. Never grow rootvg unnecessarily.

### 4. LVM mirroring
```bash
mirrorvg rootvg hdisk1
```

Redundancy for boot disk.

### 5. Monitor con topas / nmon
Real-time + recording. nmon = enterprise standard.

### 6. Snapshots antes de changes
```bash
savevg -f /tmp/rootvg.backup rootvg
```

### 7. Documentation
Each LPAR has: purpose, contacts, dependencies, SLA.

## Common issues

### 'LPAR won't boot'
- Bootlist wrong → HMC console → boot con service media
- rootvg corrupted → alt_disk_install recovery

### 'Filesystem full'
- `df -g` — identify
- `du -sh /path/*` — find culprits
- Extend: `chfs -a size=+2G /var`

### 'Performance slow'
- `topas` para overview
- `nmon` grabar 1h → analyze
- `iostat 5` — disk latency
- `lparstat 5` — CPU sharing issues

## Migración a Power10
Newer hardware requires OS level:
- Power10 needs AIX 7.2 TL5+ o AIX 7.3
- Plan LPAR migrations con Live Partition Mobility (LPM)

## Autorización
- `root` account (careful)
- `sudo` disponible pero not standard en AIX (config manually)
- HMC roles: hscroot (admin), viewer, operator

title: AIX: JFS2 + LVM avanzado
excerpt: Gestión avanzada de storage AIX con JFS2 + LVM.
body:
## AIX LVM (Logical Volume Manager)

### Hierarchy
```
Physical Volume (PV)  →  hdisk0, hdisk1, hdisk2
    ↓ grouped into
Volume Group (VG)    →  rootvg, datavg
    ↓ carved into
Logical Volume (LV)  →  hd1, hd2, lv_data
    ↓ formatted as
Filesystem (FS)      →  /home, /usr, /data
```

### Physical Volumes
```bash
# List
lspv
# Output:
# hdisk0  00c1234512345678  rootvg  active
# hdisk1  00c1234587654321  datavg  active

# Detail
lspv hdisk0

# See what LVs are on it
lspv -l hdisk0

# Physical partitions
lspv -p hdisk0
```

### Volume Groups
```bash
# List all
lsvg

# Detail
lsvg rootvg
lsvg -l rootvg     # LVs en el VG
lsvg -p rootvg     # PVs en el VG

# Create new VG
mkvg -y datavg -s 128 hdisk1 hdisk2
# -s 128 = physical partition size (MB)

# Extend con more disk
extendvg datavg hdisk3

# Reduce (drop a disk)
reducevg datavg hdisk3

# Export (unmount + remove config)
varyoffvg datavg
exportvg datavg

# Import (usually en other server)
importvg -y datavg hdisk1
varyonvg datavg
```

### Logical Volumes
```bash
# List
lslv hd1
lslv -l hd1        # PVs holding it
lslv -p hdisk0 hd1 # partition map

# Create
mklv -y lv_data -t jfs2 datavg 50G
# -t jfs2 = LV type (jfs2, jfs, sysdump, boot, jfslog, etc.)

# Mirror
mklvcopy lv_data 2 hdisk2   # add 2nd mirror on hdisk2
syncvg -l lv_data           # sync mirror

# Unmirror
rmlvcopy lv_data 1 hdisk2

# Rename
chlv -n new_name old_name

# Remove
rmlv lv_data
```

## JFS2 (Enhanced Journaled File System)
Modern AIX filesystem. JFS legacy.

### Features
- Journaling (fast fsck)
- Extended attributes
- ACLs (NFS4 ACL support)
- Encryption (JFS2 EFS)
- Compression opcional
- Snapshots
- Large file support (16 TB)

### Create
```bash
crfs -v jfs2 -d lv_data -m /data -A yes
# -v type
# -d LV
# -m mount point
# -A yes = auto-mount at boot

mount /data
```

### Extend
```bash
chfs -a size=+10G /data

# Absolute size
chfs -a size=100G /data
```

Dynamic — no unmount required.

### Reduce (JFS2 solamente en AIX 6.1+)
```bash
chfs -a size=-5G /data
```

Careful — data must fit remaining space.

### Info
```bash
df -g /data                # usage
lsfs /data                 # config
su - root -c 'fsck /data'  # check (unmounted only)
```

### Options
- `logname=INLINE` — log within LV (default JFS2)
- `agsize=64` — allocation group size (default 64MB)
- `nbpi=4096` — bytes per inode (larger = fewer inodes)

## Mirror rootvg (best practice)
```bash
# Add disk to rootvg
extendvg rootvg hdisk1

# Mirror
mirrorvg rootvg

# Sync
syncvg -v rootvg

# Update bootlist
bootlist -m normal hdisk0 hdisk1

# Also boot record
bosboot -a -d /dev/hdisk1
```

Ahora rootvg mirrored — server survives 1 disk failure.

## Snapshots
Copy-on-write point-in-time snapshot:
```bash
# Create snapshot space
snapshot -o snapfrom=/data -o size=5G

# Snapshots creados go to /data snapshot pool

# Rollback
rollback /data /path/to/snapshot
```

Útil antes de risky changes (upgrade, patch).

## Filesystem cache (mount opts)
```bash
mount -o rbrw /data                # read-behind mode (large sequential)
mount -o cio /data                 # concurrent I/O (Oracle DB)
mount -o dio /data                 # direct I/O (no cache)
```

## Alternate disk install (alt_disk)
Clone rootvg a other disk, minimal downtime for OS upgrade:

```bash
# Clone current rootvg to hdisk1
alt_disk_copy -d hdisk1

# Now hdisk1 is bootable clone

# Set bootlist a hdisk1
bootlist -m normal hdisk1

# Reboot into cloned system
shutdown -Fr

# If issues, boot from original hdisk0
```

Safe method para OS upgrades — rollback fácil.

## Storage MPIO (Multi-Path I/O)
Redundancy para SAN storage:

```bash
# List paths per hdisk
lspath
lspath -l hdisk3 -F 'name,parent,path_id,path_status,connection'

# Enable/disable path
chpath -l hdisk3 -p fscsi0 -s disable   # disable path
chpath -l hdisk3 -p fscsi0 -s enable

# Attribute (algorithm)
lsattr -El hdisk3 -a algorithm
chdev -l hdisk3 -a algorithm=round_robin

# Reserve policy
chdev -l hdisk3 -a reserve_policy=no_reserve
```

Common algorithms:
- **fail_over** — passive/active
- **round_robin** — balance across paths
- **shortest_queue** — path menos loaded

## FS quota (JFS2)
```bash
# Enable
chfs -a quota=userquota,groupquota /home

# Assign quota
edquota juan

# Reports
quotacheck /home
quota -v juan
repquota /home
```

## Compression + encryption

### Compressed LV
```bash
mkfs -V jfs2 -o compress=yes /dev/lv_data
```

### JFS2 EFS (Encrypted File System)
```bash
efsenable -a
# Users generate keys y mount encrypted FS
```

## Common issues

### 'Filesystem full pero du muestra menos'
File deleted pero abierto por proceso:
```bash
lsof +L1        # files unlinked pero abiertos
fuser -x /path  # procesos usando
```

Restart proceso o kill.

### 'VG won't varyon'
```bash
varyonvg -f datavg    # force (careful — may indicate corruption)
```

Si one disk missing: `varyonvg -o` en some situations.

### 'Slow LVM operations'
- Too many PPs (partitions) — larger PP size
- Fragmentation — reorgvg

```bash
reorgvg datavg     # rearrange for efficiency
```

### 'Cannot delete LV — in use'
```bash
umount /data
rmlv lv_data
```

Si 'device busy':
```bash
fuser -k /data     # kill users
```

## Best practices

### 1. Separate rootvg from data
Rootvg small (30-50 GB). Data en separate VGs.

### 2. Mirror rootvg
OS drive redundancy critical.

### 3. RAID via storage
Data VGs on SAN with RAID — no mirror needed en LVM level.

### 4. Regular snapshots
Before major changes.

### 5. Monitor space
```bash
df -g | awk '$4 > 80 {print}'   # >80% full
```

Alert.

### 6. Backup PV info
```bash
lspv > /backup/lspv.$(date +%F)
lsvg -l rootvg > /backup/rootvg.$(date +%F)
```

Useful para DR.

### 7. Documentation
Diagram VG/LV/FS layout per server.

## Autorización
- `root` para LVM operations
- Delegate via sudo (rare)
- HMC RBAC para virtual disk changes en VIOS

title: Linux: systemd — units, services, targets
excerpt: Gestión de servicios Linux con systemd.
body:
## systemd
Init system + service manager estándar en Linux moderno (RHEL 7+, Ubuntu 16.04+, Debian 8+).

### Reemplaza
- SysV init (`/etc/init.d/`)
- Upstart
- init scripts a mano

### Beneficios
- Parallel service startup
- Dependency management
- Cgroups integration
- Journal logging unificado
- Timers (better cron)
- Socket activation

## Unit types
- **`.service`** — daemon o process
- **`.socket`** — IPC socket
- **`.mount`** — filesystem mount
- **`.automount`** — auto-mount
- **`.timer`** — scheduled activation
- **`.target`** — group of units (like runlevel)
- **`.slice`** — cgroup slice
- **`.path`** — file path watcher
- **`.device`** — udev device
- **`.swap`** — swap file/partition

## Locations
- `/etc/systemd/system/` — local admin overrides (highest priority)
- `/run/systemd/system/` — runtime
- `/lib/systemd/system/` o `/usr/lib/systemd/system/` — distro packages

## systemctl

### Basic
```bash
systemctl start nginx
systemctl stop nginx
systemctl restart nginx
systemctl reload nginx        # SIGHUP — reload config sin restart
systemctl status nginx

systemctl enable nginx        # auto-start at boot
systemctl disable nginx
systemctl is-enabled nginx
systemctl is-active nginx
```

### List
```bash
systemctl list-units                       # active units
systemctl list-units --type=service        # only services
systemctl list-units --all                 # inactive too
systemctl list-unit-files                  # installed + enabled state
systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled
```

### Failed
```bash
systemctl --failed
```

Muestra units en failed state.

### Reset failed
```bash
systemctl reset-failed nginx
```

Clears failed state (for retry).

## Journal (systemd-journald)

### Ver logs
```bash
journalctl                          # todo el journal
journalctl -u nginx                 # unit específica
journalctl -u nginx -f              # follow (like tail -f)
journalctl -u nginx --since '10 min ago'
journalctl -u nginx --since '2026-07-01' --until '2026-07-15'

journalctl -p err                   # solo errores + up
journalctl -p 3                     # (0=emerg, 3=err, 6=info, 7=debug)

journalctl --list-boots             # boots recorded
journalctl -b -1                    # previous boot
journalctl -k                       # only kernel messages
```

### Persistent journal
By default puede ser volátil (`/run/log/journal`).

Enable persistent:
```bash
sudo mkdir -p /var/log/journal
sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
```

### Size limit
Edit `/etc/systemd/journald.conf`:
```
SystemMaxUse=1G
SystemMaxFileSize=100M
MaxRetentionSec=1month
```

Apply:
```bash
sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
```

### Rotate
```bash
sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M    # keep only 500MB
sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=7d      # keep only last 7 days
```

## Crear service unit

### Ejemplo `/etc/systemd/system/myapp.service`
```ini
[Unit]
Description=My Application
Documentation=https://empresa.local/docs/myapp
After=network.target postgresql.service
Requires=postgresql.service

[Service]
Type=simple
User=myapp
Group=myapp
WorkingDirectory=/opt/myapp
Environment='NODE_ENV=production'
EnvironmentFile=/opt/myapp/.env
ExecStart=/opt/myapp/bin/start.sh
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
ExecStop=/opt/myapp/bin/stop.sh
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
StandardOutput=append:/var/log/myapp/stdout.log
StandardError=append:/var/log/myapp/stderr.log

# Security hardening
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
ReadWritePaths=/var/log/myapp /opt/myapp/data
PrivateTmp=yes
CapabilityBoundingSet=
AmbientCapabilities=

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

### Service Types
- **simple** (default) — ExecStart es el main process
- **forking** — process forks + parent exits (legacy daemons)
- **oneshot** — runs once + exits (like init script)
- **notify** — service notifies systemd cuando ready (via `sd_notify()`)
- **dbus** — service registered on DBus
- **idle** — waits until other boot activity done

### Enable + start
```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable myapp
sudo systemctl start myapp
```

## Timers (reemplazo de cron)

### `/etc/systemd/system/cleanup.service`
```ini
[Unit]
Description=Cleanup old files

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh
```

### `/etc/systemd/system/cleanup.timer`
```ini
[Unit]
Description=Run cleanup daily

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
OnCalendar=03:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

### Enable
```bash
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now cleanup.timer

# Ver timers
systemctl list-timers
```

### Calendar syntax
- `daily` — 00:00 every day
- `weekly` — Monday 00:00
- `monthly` — 1st day 00:00
- `Mon..Fri 09:00` — weekdays 9AM
- `*-*-* 03:00:00` — every day 3AM
- `hourly`
- `*-*-1..15 10:00` — 1st-15th of month at 10AM

Persistent: si machine off durante trigger, runs at boot.

## Targets (runlevels)

### Equivalencias
- **poweroff.target** — runlevel 0
- **rescue.target** — runlevel 1 (single-user)
- **multi-user.target** — runlevel 3 (CLI multi-user)
- **graphical.target** — runlevel 5 (GUI)
- **reboot.target** — runlevel 6

### Change default
```bash
systemctl get-default
sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target
```

### Change current
```bash
sudo systemctl isolate rescue.target
```

## Dependencies

### Types
- **Requires=** — hard dependency (fails if not up)
- **Wants=** — soft dependency (nice to have)
- **After=** — order (start after X)
- **Before=** — order (start before X)
- **Conflicts=** — cannot run together

### View
```bash
systemctl list-dependencies nginx
systemctl list-dependencies nginx --reverse  # who depends on nginx
```

## Override configs (no touch upstream)

### Drop-in directory
```bash
sudo systemctl edit nginx
```

Creates `/etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/override.conf`:
```ini
[Service]
Restart=always
RestartSec=10s
```

Solo campos a change. Merges con upstream unit.

### Full override
```bash
sudo systemctl edit --full nginx
```

Copies entire unit a `/etc/systemd/system/` para modificar.

### Revert
```bash
sudo systemctl revert nginx
```

Remueve overrides.

## Cgroups + resources

### Limit CPU/memory
```ini
[Service]
CPUQuota=200%           # 2 cores max
MemoryMax=1G
TasksMax=100
```

O runtime:
```bash
sudo systemctl set-property nginx MemoryMax=500M
```

### Ver usage
```bash
systemd-cgtop
systemctl status nginx    # incluye CPU + memory
```

## Boot analysis

### Boot time
```bash
systemd-analyze                        # total time
systemd-analyze blame                  # per-unit time
systemd-analyze critical-chain         # critical path
systemd-analyze plot > boot.svg        # visual timeline
```

## Security hardening
Production services should include:
```ini
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict           # /usr, /boot, /efi read-only
ProtectHome=yes                # /home, /root, /run/user hidden
PrivateTmp=yes                 # separate /tmp
PrivateDevices=yes             # no /dev access
ProtectKernelTunables=yes      # no /proc/sys writes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
LockPersonality=yes
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
CapabilityBoundingSet=
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
```

Audit con `systemd-analyze security nginx`.

## Common issues

### 'Unit not found'
- File not en systemd path
- `daemon-reload` after creating
- Typo en filename

### 'Failed to start'
- Check `systemctl status <name>`
- Read journalctl -u <name>
- Verify ExecStart path executable

### 'Restart loop'
```ini
[Service]
Restart=on-failure
StartLimitInterval=60s
StartLimitBurst=3          # max 3 restarts in 60s, then give up
```

### 'Service starts but nothing happens'
- Wrong Type= (forking vs simple)
- ExecStart returns immediately
- Add logging inside script

## Best practices

### 1. Custom units en /etc/systemd/system/
Not en /lib/... (package files, get overwritten).

### 2. Documentation field
Each unit has Documentation= URL.

### 3. Restart policies
- `on-failure` para crashes
- `always` para long-running daemons

### 4. Journal for logs
Over custom log files. Unified query.

### 5. Timers over cron
Better dependency + logging.

### 6. Security hardening
Especially for network-facing services.

### 7. Resource limits
Avoid runaway processes killing server.

## Autorización
- `root` para system units
- User services en `~/.config/systemd/user/` (per-user, no root)

title: Linux: LVM + filesystems (ext4, XFS)
tags: linux, lvm, ext4, xfs, filesystem, storage
body:
## Linux LVM
Logical Volume Manager — abstraction layer sobre discos:
- Resize dinámico
- Snapshots
- Multi-disk pooling
- Migration in-place

### Hierarchy
```
Physical Volume (PV)  →  /dev/sdb, /dev/sdc
    ↓
Volume Group (VG)    →  vg_data
    ↓
Logical Volume (LV)  →  lv_home, lv_var
    ↓
Filesystem           →  formatted ext4/xfs
```

## Basic setup

### 1. Create PV
```bash
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
```

### 2. Create VG
```bash
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
```

### 3. Create LV
```bash
sudo lvcreate -n lv_home -L 100G vg_data
# o -l 100%FREE para todo el free space
```

### 4. Filesystem
```bash
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/vg_data/lv_home
# o mkfs.xfs /dev/vg_data/lv_home
```

### 5. Mount
```bash
sudo mkdir /home
sudo mount /dev/vg_data/lv_home /home

# Persistent en /etc/fstab
echo '/dev/vg_data/lv_home /home ext4 defaults 0 2' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
```

## Inspection
```bash
pvs               # PVs
pvdisplay

vgs               # VGs
vgdisplay vg_data

lvs               # LVs
lvdisplay /dev/vg_data/lv_home

df -h             # mounts + usage
lsblk             # block devices tree
```

## Extend LV + filesystem

### 1. Extend VG (si necesitas más espacio)
```bash
sudo pvcreate /dev/sdd
sudo vgextend vg_data /dev/sdd
```

### 2. Extend LV
```bash
sudo lvextend -L +50G /dev/vg_data/lv_home
# o -l +100%FREE
```

### 3. Extend filesystem
**ext4:**
```bash
sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_home
```

**XFS:**
```bash
sudo xfs_growfs /home
```

Online (no unmount) para ambos.

### One-shot con `-r`
```bash
sudo lvextend -L +50G -r /dev/vg_data/lv_home
```

`-r` auto-resizes filesystem.

## Shrink LV (ext4 only)
XFS NO permite shrink. Only ext4.

### Steps (careful, data must fit new size)
```bash
sudo umount /home
sudo e2fsck -f /dev/vg_data/lv_home
sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_home 50G       # shrink FS first
sudo lvreduce -L 50G /dev/vg_data/lv_home     # then LV
sudo mount /home
```

Order critical — FS before LV o corruption.

## Snapshots
Point-in-time frozen view del LV. Uses copy-on-write.

### Create
```bash
sudo lvcreate -s -n snap_home -L 10G /dev/vg_data/lv_home
```

`-L 10G` = espacio para changes. Si excede, snapshot invalidates.

### Mount snapshot (read-only recommended)
```bash
sudo mkdir /mnt/snap
sudo mount -o ro /dev/vg_data/snap_home /mnt/snap
```

### Rollback
```bash
sudo umount /home
sudo lvconvert --merge /dev/vg_data/snap_home
sudo mount /home    # ahora es el estado del snapshot
```

### Remove
```bash
sudo umount /mnt/snap
sudo lvremove /dev/vg_data/snap_home
```

## Filesystems

### ext4
- Mature, universal support
- Max FS size: 1 EiB (theoretical), 50 TB (typical)
- Max file: 16 TiB
- Fast fsck
- Journal (data=ordered default)

#### Options
```bash
sudo mkfs.ext4 -L data -b 4096 -m 1 /dev/vg_data/lv_data
# -L label
# -b block size (4096 default)
# -m 1% reserved for root (default 5%)
```

#### Tune existing
```bash
sudo tune2fs -l /dev/vg_data/lv_data       # ver params
sudo tune2fs -m 1 /dev/vg_data/lv_data     # cambiar reserved
sudo tune2fs -c 30 -i 6m /dev/vg_data/lv_data   # fsck after 30 mounts o 6 months
```

### XFS
- Modern, high performance
- Max FS size: 8 EiB
- Max file: 8 EiB
- Better parallelism
- Grow-only (no shrink)
- Default en RHEL 7+

#### Options
```bash
sudo mkfs.xfs -L data -b size=4096 /dev/vg_data/lv_data
```

#### Repair
```bash
sudo xfs_repair /dev/vg_data/lv_data    # only unmounted
```

#### Info
```bash
sudo xfs_info /data
```

### Comparison
| Feature | ext4 | XFS |
|---------|------|-----|
| Max FS | 1 EiB | 8 EiB |
| Shrink | Yes | No |
| Snapshot native | No (via LVM) | No (via LVM) |
| Journal | Yes | Yes |
| Default RHEL | 6 | 7+ |
| Default Ubuntu | Yes | Optional |
| Performance | Good | Best (parallel) |
| Recovery time | Slow (large FS) | Fast |

## Mount options
```
/dev/vg_data/lv_home /home ext4 defaults,noatime,nodiratime 0 2
```

### Common
- `noatime` — don't update access times (perf boost)
- `nodiratime` — same for dirs
- `discard` — TRIM for SSD (auto)
- `ro` — read-only
- `nosuid` — ignore SUID bits
- `noexec` — no execute permission
- `nodev` — no device files

### Security hardening
For `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/dev/shm`:
```
/dev/vg_data/lv_tmp /tmp ext4 defaults,noexec,nosuid,nodev 0 2
```

Prevents execution of malicious scripts from /tmp.

### For SSDs
```
/dev/nvme0n1p2 / ext4 defaults,discard,noatime 0 1
```

`discard` sends TRIM commands automatically.

### For DBs
```
/dev/vg_data/lv_db /var/lib/postgresql ext4 defaults,noatime,data=writeback 0 2
```

`data=writeback` = fastest (mais unsafe on power loss — DB has own WAL).

## RAID + LVM
LVM can span RAID:
- Hardware RAID → 1 disk visible to Linux → PV on that
- Or software RAID (mdadm) → md device → PV on that

### mdadm RAID 1
```bash
sudo mdadm --create /dev/md0 --level=1 --raid-devices=2 /dev/sdb /dev/sdc
sudo pvcreate /dev/md0
sudo vgcreate vg_data /dev/md0
```

RAID handles redundancy, LVM handles logical carve-up.

### LVM RAID (built-in)
```bash
sudo lvcreate --type raid1 -m 1 -L 100G -n lv_data vg_data
```

`-m 1` = 1 mirror (2 copies total).

## LVM thin provisioning
Over-commit storage — allocate ondemand:

### Create thin pool
```bash
sudo lvcreate -L 500G --thinpool tp_data vg_data
```

### Create thin LVs
```bash
sudo lvcreate -V 200G -T vg_data/tp_data -n lv_a
sudo lvcreate -V 200G -T vg_data/tp_data -n lv_b
sudo lvcreate -V 200G -T vg_data/tp_data -n lv_c
# 600G virtual > 500G pool, pero solo usan lo que escriben
```

### Warning
Monitor pool usage — cuando pool full, writes fail:
```bash
lvs vg_data/tp_data       # Data% shows fill
```

Alert @ 80%.

## Migration
Move LV a diferente PV:
```bash
sudo pvmove /dev/sdb /dev/sdd
```

Moves all data desde sdb a sdd. Online. Slow (large data).

### Después remove old PV
```bash
sudo vgreduce vg_data /dev/sdb
sudo pvremove /dev/sdb
```

## Common issues

### 'Cannot extend LV — no space'
```bash
vgs             # check VG free space
sudo vgextend vg_data /dev/sdd    # add more disk
```

### 'Filesystem grew but LV didn't extend'
```bash
sudo lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg_data/lv_home
sudo resize2fs /dev/vg_data/lv_home
```

### 'Cannot mount — bad superblock'
```bash
sudo e2fsck -b 32768 /dev/vg_data/lv_home    # try alternate superblock
```

### 'Snapshot invalidated'
Exceeded snapshot size:
```bash
sudo lvextend -L +5G /dev/vg_data/snap_home    # if not too late
```

Allocate more space initially next time.

### 'PV missing after boot'
- Cable/disk failure
- `sudo vgchange -a y` para active vgs
- Or `sudo lvchange -a y` per LV

## Best practices

### 1. LVM everywhere
Even single disks — future flexibility.

### 2. Standard layout
- `/boot` — separate partition, no LVM (typically /dev/sda1)
- `/` — LV lv_root
- `/home` — LV lv_home
- `/var` — LV lv_var
- `/var/log` — LV lv_varlog (optional)
- swap — LV lv_swap

### 3. Reserve space
Leave some free en VG for growth + snapshots.

### 4. XFS por default
Modern default. Fast, scalable. Only ext4 si need shrink.

### 5. Snapshots antes de risky ops
System upgrade, DB restore, app deployment.

### 6. Backup includes LVM structure
```bash
sudo vgcfgbackup vg_data      # backup metadata to /etc/lvm/backup/
```

### 7. Monitor
```bash
df -h | awk '$5 >= '90%' {print}'
```

Alert.

## Autorización
- `root` para LVM operations
- `sudo` typical
- Non-root users can view (`pvs`, `vgs`, `lvs` sometimes require sudo depending on distro)

title: Linux: SELinux troubleshooting
excerpt: SELinux troubleshooting — audit logs, contexts, booleans.
body:
## SELinux
Security-Enhanced Linux — MAC (Mandatory Access Control):
- Every process + file has security context
- Kernel enforces policies
- Complements DAC (traditional Unix perms)

### Modes
- **Enforcing** — policies enforced (production)
- **Permissive** — policies not enforced, but violations logged (testing)
- **Disabled** — SELinux off (not recommended)

### Ver mode
```bash
getenforce
sestatus
```

### Change mode
```bash
sudo setenforce 0        # permissive (temp)
sudo setenforce 1        # enforcing (temp)
```

Permanent: edit `/etc/selinux/config`:
```
SELINUX=enforcing
SELINUXTYPE=targeted
```

Reboot required to change enforcing ↔ disabled.

## Context format
```
user:role:type:level
```

Ejemplo:
- `system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0`
- `unconfined_u:unconfined_r:unconfined_t:s0-s0:c0.c1023`

**Type** es el más importante para debugging.

## Ver contexts

### Files
```bash
ls -Z /var/www/html
# -rw-r--r--. root root system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 index.html
```

### Processes
```bash
ps -eZ | grep httpd
# system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0     1234  ?     httpd
```

### Users
```bash
id -Z
# unconfined_u:unconfined_r:unconfined_t:s0-s0:c0.c1023
```

## Common denials

### Log location
Most distros: `/var/log/audit/audit.log`

### Search denials
```bash
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts today
sudo ausearch -m avc -c httpd    # solo httpd denials
```

### Human-readable
```bash
sudo sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log
# Or si setroubleshoot instalado:
sudo sealert --html-report -a /var/log/audit/audit.log > report.html
```

## Fix approaches

### 1. Wrong context
Ejemplo: files copiados a `/var/www/html` con context wrong.

```bash
sudo ls -Z index.html
# -rw-r--r--. root root unconfined_u:object_r:admin_home_t:s0 index.html
```

Fix con `restorecon`:
```bash
sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html
```

Restores default context per file_contexts config.

### 2. New location — add rule
Si apache should serve desde `/webapp` (non-standard):
```bash
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/webapp(/.*)?'
sudo restorecon -Rv /webapp
```

Permanent rule.

### 3. Ver contexts esperados
```bash
sudo semanage fcontext -l | grep webapp
```

## Ports
Bind non-standard port bloqueado por SELinux.

### Ver puertos permitidos para type
```bash
sudo semanage port -l | grep http
# http_port_t   tcp   80, 81, 443, 488, 8008, 8009, 8443, 9000
```

### Add port
```bash
sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8888
```

Ahora Apache puede bind a 8888.

### Modify existing (si conflicto)
```bash
sudo semanage port -m -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080
```

### Remove
```bash
sudo semanage port -d -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080
```

## Booleans
Toggles pre-defined en policy.

### Ver todos
```bash
getsebool -a
# httpd_can_network_connect --> off
# httpd_enable_homedirs --> off
# ...
```

### Buscar
```bash
sudo semanage boolean -l | grep httpd
```

### Toggle
```bash
# Temporary
sudo setsebool httpd_can_network_connect on

# Persistent
sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
```

### Common booleans útiles
- `httpd_can_network_connect` — Apache can make outbound connections
- `httpd_can_network_connect_db` — Apache can connect to DB
- `httpd_enable_homedirs` — serve from home directories
- `httpd_execmem` — allow certain exec patterns
- `samba_export_all_ro` / `samba_export_all_rw` — samba shares
- `ftpd_full_access`
- `nis_enabled`

## Debugging workflow

### 1. Aplicación falla — is it SELinux?
```bash
# Set permissive temporary
sudo setenforce 0

# Retry app

# If ahora works → SELinux issue
```

### 2. Set back to enforcing
```bash
sudo setenforce 1
```

### 3. Trigger the error + capture
```bash
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent
```

### 4. Analyze
```bash
sudo sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log | tail -100
```

Output ejemplo:
```
SELinux is preventing httpd from write access on the file /var/www/html/uploads/file.txt.

*****  Plugin catchall_labels (83.8 confidence) suggests   *****

If you want to allow httpd to have write access on the file file.txt
Then you need to change the label on file.txt.

Do:
# semanage fcontext -a -t FILE_TYPE 'file.txt'
# restorecon -v 'file.txt'
```

### 5. Apply fix suggested
Restorecon, or add fcontext rule, or toggle boolean, etc.

## Custom policy modules

Si denial legítimo pero no cubierto por defaults, create module:

### 1. Capture recent denials + generate policy
```bash
sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent | audit2allow -M myapp
# genera myapp.te + myapp.pp
```

### 2. Review .te (text policy)
```bash
cat myapp.te
# module myapp 1.0;
# require {
#     type httpd_t;
#     type samba_share_t;
#     class file { read write };
# }
# allow httpd_t samba_share_t:file { read write };
```

Verify no over-permissive.

### 3. Install
```bash
sudo semodule -i myapp.pp
```

### 4. Ver modules loaded
```bash
sudo semodule -l | grep myapp
```

### 5. Remove
```bash
sudo semodule -r myapp
```

## Types comunes
- `httpd_t` — Apache process
- `httpd_sys_content_t` — files Apache reads
- `httpd_sys_rw_content_t` — files Apache reads + writes
- `mysqld_t`
- `postgresql_t`
- `ssh_t`
- `sshd_t`
- `user_t` — normal users
- `staff_t` — power users
- `admin_home_t` — root's home
- `bin_t` — /usr/bin executables
- `var_log_t` — /var/log

## file_contexts
See default context rules:
```bash
cat /etc/selinux/targeted/contexts/files/file_contexts
```

Regex-based — first match wins.

## semanage user

Map Linux users → SELinux users:
```bash
sudo semanage login -l
sudo semanage login -a -s user_u alice   # alice → user_u (restricted)
```

By default, users → unconfined_u (usually).

## Common issues

### 'Cannot bind port'
- Check `semanage port -l`
- Add port a corresponding type

### 'Cannot read/write file'
- Check `ls -Z` context
- `restorecon` if standard location
- Add `semanage fcontext` rule if custom

### 'Cannot connect to DB'
- Boolean `httpd_can_network_connect_db` off (typical)
- Enable: `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on`

### 'Cannot execute script'
- Wrong type (script needs exec type)
- `chcon -t httpd_sys_script_exec_t script.cgi`

### 'AVC denials but app works'
- May be silent failures — check logs of app
- Or app has fallback (usually not)
- Fix anyway to prevent future breaks

### 'Denials después de restart / reboot'
- Contexts not persistent
- `restorecon -Rv` no aplicado permanently
- Use `semanage fcontext -a` for permanent

## Best practices

### 1. Never disable SELinux
Enforcing por default. Permissive solo temp para debugging.

### 2. Use targeted policy
`SELINUXTYPE=targeted` — standard. `mls` (multi-level) only para high-security envs.

### 3. Use semanage over chcon
chcon temporary — lost after relabel.
semanage permanent.

### 4. Restorecon after changes
`restorecon -Rv /path` — safe reset.

### 5. Understand booleans first
Most app issues resolved via boolean toggle. No need custom module.

### 6. Custom modules signed + version-controlled
Don't just install random .pp files.

### 7. Log AVCs a SIEM
Security teams need visibility.

### 8. Test permissive mode antes de deploy
Use `permissive <type>` para specific processes:
```bash
sudo semanage permissive -a httpd_t
```

Solo ese type permissive, rest enforcing.

### 9. audit2allow with scrutiny
Don't blindly accept. Review .te carefully. Over-permissive rules defeat purpose.

## Autorización
- `root` para setenforce, semanage, semodule
- Users con `_r_u` role — restringidos por default
- Delegated con sudo rules

title: Linux: firewalld + nftables config
body:
## Firewall en Linux moderno

### Layers
- **iptables** (legacy) — old CLI, still valid en older systems
- **nftables** — new native kernel firewall (since Linux 3.13)
- **firewalld** — dynamic zone-based firewall (RHEL default) — uses nftables underneath
- **ufw** — Ubuntu-friendly wrapper (uses iptables/nftables)

## firewalld
En RHEL/CentOS/Fedora por default.

### Enable
```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now firewalld
sudo firewall-cmd --state
```

### Zones
Grupos de rules aplicables a interfaces/networks:
- **drop** — deny all incoming, no reply
- **block** — deny all incoming with rejection
- **public** (default) — untrusted networks, limited services
- **external** — NAT config
- **dmz** — DMZ zone (limited access allowed)
- **work** — work networks (más trust)
- **home** — home network
- **internal** — internal LAN
- **trusted** — full trust (allow all)

### Assign interface a zone
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --get-zone-of-interface=eth0
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=trusted --change-interface=eth0 --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
```

### Ver current config
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all                         # active zone
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all-zones                   # all
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --get-default-zone
```

### Change default zone
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=work
```

## Services
firewalld includes pre-defined services.

### List
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --get-services
# Ver detalles
sudo firewall-cmd --info-service=http
```

### Allow service
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=ssh --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
```

**Sin --permanent**: solo aplica hasta reboot.

### Remove
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --remove-service=http --permanent
```

### Custom service
```bash
# /etc/firewalld/services/myapp.xml
<?xml version='1.0' encoding='utf-8'?>
<service>
    <short>MyApp</short>
    <description>My custom application</description>
    <port protocol='tcp' port='8888'/>
</service>

sudo firewall-cmd --reload
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=myapp --permanent
```

## Ports directo
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=8080/tcp --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=5000-5100/tcp --permanent    # range
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-ports
```

## Source-based rules

### Allow specific IP/subnet
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=trusted --add-source=10.0.0.0/8 --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
```

Ahora traffic from 10.0.0.0/8 goes to trusted zone (allow all).

### Rich rules
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.5" service name="ssh" accept' --permanent

sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" port port="3306" protocol="tcp" accept' --permanent

sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="1.2.3.4" drop' --permanent
```

### List rich rules
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-rich-rules
```

## Port forwarding + masquerading

### Enable masquerade (NAT)
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=external --add-masquerade --permanent
```

### Forward port
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=external --add-forward-port=port=80:proto=tcp:toport=8080:toaddr=10.0.0.10 --permanent
```

Traffic to server:80 → forwarded to 10.0.0.10:8080.

## Log denied
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --set-log-denied=all
```

Logs to /var/log/messages (o journal).

## Panic mode
Drop ALL traffic (emergency):
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --panic-on
# emergency + investigation
sudo firewall-cmd --panic-off
```

## nftables (native)
Modern replacement of iptables:

### Ver rules
```bash
sudo nft list ruleset
```

### Basic config `/etc/nftables.conf`
```
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

flush ruleset

table inet filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
        
        # Allow loopback
        iif lo accept
        
        # Allow established/related
        ct state established,related accept
        
        # Allow ICMP
        ip protocol icmp accept
        ip6 nexthdr ipv6-icmp accept
        
        # Allow SSH
        tcp dport 22 accept
        
        # Allow HTTP/HTTPS
        tcp dport { 80, 443 } accept
        
        # Log + drop rest
        log prefix 'DROP: ' limit rate 5/minute
        counter drop
    }
    
    chain forward {
        type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
    }
    
    chain output {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;
    }
}
```

### Apply
```bash
sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf
sudo systemctl enable --now nftables
```

### CLI operations
```bash
# Add rule dynamically
sudo nft add rule inet filter input tcp dport 8080 accept

# Delete
sudo nft list chain inet filter input -a       # show con handles
sudo nft delete rule inet filter input handle 5

# Add table + chain
sudo nft add table inet mytable
sudo nft add chain inet mytable mychain { type filter hook input priority 0\; }

# Save current a file
sudo nft list ruleset > /etc/nftables.conf
```

### Sets (grouped values)
```
table inet filter {
    set trusted_ips {
        type ipv4_addr
        elements = { 10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.5, 192.168.1.100 }
    }
    
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
        ip saddr @trusted_ips accept
    }
}
```

Dynamic add:
```bash
sudo nft add element inet filter trusted_ips { 1.2.3.4 }
```

### Maps (key-value)
```
table inet filter {
    map port_forward {
        type inet_service : ipv4_addr
        elements = { 80 : 10.0.0.10, 443 : 10.0.0.11 }
    }
}
```

## iptables (legacy)
Still supported. `iptables` command generates nftables rules en RHEL 8+.

### Basic
```bash
sudo iptables -L -v -n            # list
sudo iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
sudo iptables -A INPUT -s 10.0.0.5 -j DROP

# Save
sudo iptables-save > /etc/iptables/rules.v4
```

En RHEL 8+, iptables-nft translates a nftables internamente.

## Firewalld vs raw nftables

### firewalld pros
- Dynamic changes sin flush
- Zone-based abstraction
- Predefined services
- Runtime + permanent separate
- Rich rule syntax

### nftables pros
- Faster (native kernel)
- More flexible (sets, maps, dynamic)
- Complex rulesets easier
- Modern syntax

### Recommendation
- **Simple servers**: firewalld
- **Complex networks (firewalls, gateways)**: raw nftables
- **RHEL default**: firewalld (uses nftables underneath)

## Common issues

### 'Puerto abierto pero no accessible desde afuera'
- Check zone: `firewall-cmd --list-all`
- Service allowed en right zone?
- Interface en right zone?
- Cloud provider security group también blocking (AWS SG, Azure NSG, GCP firewall)?

### 'ssh me sacó del servidor'
Added rule accidentally denying SSH. Console access needed.

**Prevention**: use `--timeout=60` para test rules:
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=ssh --timeout=60
```

Si no confirm, revert después de 60s.

### 'Changes not persisting'
- Missed `--permanent`
- Missed `--reload`
- Wrong zone modified

### 'Docker rules conflicting'
Docker manipulates iptables. Conflicts con firewalld.

Solutions:
- Disable Docker iptables: `--iptables=false` (breaks Docker networking)
- Better: use firewalld with docker zone

### 'fail2ban + firewalld'
fail2ban integration: config para use firewalld backend:
```
# /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
banaction = firewallcmd-multiport
```

## Best practices

### 1. Default deny
Drop unmatched traffic. Only explicit allow.

### 2. Least privilege
Minimum ports open. Every rule justified.

### 3. Log denied
Monitor for scanning / brute force.

### 4. Rate limit
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule service name="ssh" limit value="5/m" accept' --permanent
```

Max 5 SSH connections/min per source.

### 5. Fail2ban con firewall
Ban repeat offenders automatically.

### 6. Version control config
`/etc/firewalld/` o `/etc/nftables.conf` en git.

### 7. Test antes de reboot
Rules loaded correctly? `firewall-cmd --list-all`.

### 8. Emergency access
SSH access via IPMI/console si firewall locks you out.

### 9. Ansible/Puppet manage
Don't manually add rules. Config management ensures consistency.

### 10. Regular audit
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all-zones > firewall-config.txt
```

Monthly review — what's really needed?

## Autorización
- `root` para firewall changes
- Delegated via sudo rules
- Consider RBAC roles

title: Linux: SSSD + LDAP client integration
tags: sssd, ldap, ad, kerberos, linux, auth
excerpt: Integrar Linux con AD/LDAP para auth centralizada.
body:
## SSSD (System Security Services Daemon)
Centraliza auth Linux → AD/LDAP:
- Users can login con AD credentials
- Group membership honored
- Cached credentials para offline
- Kerberos SSO
- Multiple auth providers

## Setup con AD

### 1. Install packages (RHEL)
```bash
sudo dnf install -y realmd sssd oddjob oddjob-mkhomedir adcli samba-common-tools
```

Ubuntu:
```bash
sudo apt install -y realmd sssd sssd-tools libnss-sss libpam-sss adcli samba-common-bin oddjob oddjob-mkhomedir packagekit
```

### 2. Discover domain
```bash
sudo realm discover empresa.local
```

Output muestra domain, forest, servers.

### 3. Join domain
```bash
sudo realm join --user=admin@EMPRESA.LOCAL empresa.local
```

Enter admin password. Server aparece en AD como computer object.

### 4. Verify
```bash
sudo realm list

id alice@empresa.local           # test lookup
getent passwd alice@empresa.local
```

### 5. Login test
```bash
ssh alice@empresa.local@localhost
```

Default, all AD users can login. Restrict later.

## SSSD config `/etc/sssd/sssd.conf`
```ini
[sssd]
domains = empresa.local
config_file_version = 2
services = nss, pam, ssh, sudo

[domain/empresa.local]
id_provider = ad
auth_provider = ad
access_provider = ad
chpass_provider = ad

ad_domain = empresa.local
ad_server = dc1.empresa.local, dc2.empresa.local
ad_gpo_access_control = permissive

krb5_realm = EMPRESA.LOCAL
realmd_tags = manages-system joined-with-adcli

cache_credentials = true
krb5_store_password_if_offline = true
default_shell = /bin/bash
fallback_homedir = /home/%u
use_fully_qualified_names = true
ldap_id_mapping = true

# Access control (opcional — restrict login)
access_provider = simple
simple_allow_groups = linux_admins@empresa.local, developers@empresa.local
```

### Permissions
```bash
sudo chmod 600 /etc/sssd/sssd.conf
sudo chown root:root /etc/sssd/sssd.conf
```

### Restart
```bash
sudo systemctl restart sssd
```

## NSS + PAM

### NSS (Name Service Switch) `/etc/nsswitch.conf`
```
passwd:     files sss
group:      files sss
shadow:     files sss
sudoers:    files sss
```

Lookup order: local `/etc/passwd`, then SSSD.

### PAM (Pluggable Authentication Modules)
realm/authconfig configures automatically. Files en `/etc/pam.d/`:
- `system-auth`
- `password-auth`
- `sssd-shadowutils`

### Auto home directory
On first login, create home dir automáticamente:
```bash
sudo authselect select sssd with-mkhomedir
sudo systemctl enable --now oddjobd
```

## Restrict access

### Only specific groups
```ini
[domain/empresa.local]
access_provider = simple
simple_allow_groups = linux_admins@empresa.local, developers@empresa.local
```

Solo miembros de esos grupos → login.

### Only specific users
```ini
simple_allow_users = admin1@empresa.local, admin2@empresa.local
```

### Deny specific
```ini
simple_deny_groups = contractors@empresa.local
```

### Or via realm
```bash
sudo realm permit -g linux_admins@empresa.local
sudo realm permit alice@empresa.local
sudo realm deny --all
```

## Sudo integration

### Sudo rules stored en AD/LDAP (advanced)
Config LDAP schema para sudo:
```ini
[sssd]
services = nss, pam, sudo

[sudo]

[domain/empresa.local]
sudo_provider = ldap
ldap_sudo_search_base = ou=SUDOers,dc=empresa,dc=local
```

### Sudo rules locales (simpler)
```bash
# /etc/sudoers.d/ad_admins
%linux_admins@empresa.local ALL=(ALL) ALL
```

Any member of AD group `linux_admins` → sudo.

## Kerberos

### Verify tickets
After login:
```bash
klist
```

Muestra Kerberos tickets. Usado for SSO to other services.

### Manual auth
```bash
kinit alice@EMPRESA.LOCAL
klist
kdestroy
```

### SSH GSS-API SSO
Config `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`:
```
GSSAPIAuthentication yes
GSSAPIDelegateCredentials yes
```

Y server `/etc/ssh/sshd_config`:
```
GSSAPIAuthentication yes
```

Ahora `ssh server.empresa.local` — no password (Kerberos SSO).

## Cache management

### Ver cached users
```bash
sudo sss_cache -E                 # invalidate everything (force re-lookup)
sudo sss_cache -u alice           # invalidate specific user
sudo sss_cache -g developers      # invalidate specific group
```

After cache invalidation, next lookup hits AD.

### Ver current cache
```bash
sudo sssctl domain-list
sudo sssctl user-checks alice@empresa.local
sudo sssctl user-show alice@empresa.local
```

## Common issues

### 'Cannot join realm'
- DNS issue: server can't resolve AD DCs
  - `nslookup empresa.local`
  - Fix /etc/resolv.conf con AD DCs as nameservers
- Time skew: Kerberos requires <5 min
  - `sudo chronyc sources` — verify NTP
  - Manually sync: `sudo chronyc -a makestep`
- Firewall: allow LDAP (389/636), Kerberos (88), DNS (53), etc.

### 'User exists in AD but not visible en Linux'
- SSSD cache stale: `sudo sss_cache -E`
- Filter en sssd.conf excluding user
- `use_fully_qualified_names=true` — must use `alice@empresa.local`, not just `alice`

### 'Group members not resolved'
- Nested groups: SSSD needs correct config
- `ldap_group_nesting_level` — default 2
- `ignore_group_members=false` — enable nesting

### 'Auth fails but user exists'
- Ver `journalctl -u sssd -f` durante login attempt
- Common: `Access denied` — user not in access list
- Kerberos issue: time skew, ticket forwarding

### 'Login lento'
- Multiple AD servers not reachable
- Configure prioritized list:
```ini
ad_server = dc-fast.empresa.local, dc-backup.empresa.local
```
- Enable offline cached auth durante network issues

### 'Home dir not created'
- oddjobd not running: `sudo systemctl start oddjobd`
- PAM misconfigured: `sudo authselect select sssd with-mkhomedir`

## Alternative: winbind
Samba's tool para AD integration:
- Older, less recommended para new deployments
- SSSD preferred

Winbind still used in some legacy Samba file server setups.

## LDAP direct (no AD)
Si environment tiene LDAP puro (OpenLDAP, 389 DS, etc.):

```ini
[sssd]
domains = ldap.empresa.local

[domain/ldap.empresa.local]
id_provider = ldap
auth_provider = ldap
chpass_provider = ldap

ldap_uri = ldaps://ldap.empresa.local
ldap_search_base = dc=empresa,dc=local
ldap_tls_cacertdir = /etc/openldap/cacerts
ldap_tls_reqcert = demand

cache_credentials = true
```

## Best practices

### 1. Use AD if available
SSSD talks AD natively. Better than IPA/OpenLDAP mixed setups.

### 2. Restrict login
`access_provider = simple` con specific groups. Don't let every AD user login to every server.

### 3. Local root emergency account
Maintain local root o admin account:
```bash
sudo passwd root
```

If AD/SSSD breaks, still can login via console.

### 4. Time sync mandatory
Chrony/NTP required. Kerberos 5-min tolerance.

### 5. DNS proper
Linux server should have AD DCs en /etc/resolv.conf.

### 6. Cache backup
SSSD cache en `/var/lib/sss/db/`. Not usually needed pero puede rebuild-si-corrupted.

### 7. Logging
```ini
[sssd]
debug_level = 6
```

When troubleshooting. Return a 0 en normal ops.

### 8. Monitor cache
Huge cache si many groups/users. Rotate/clear periódicamente.

### 9. LDAP over TLS/SSL
`ldap_uri = ldaps://...` (port 636) — encrypted.

### 10. Automation
Ansible module `ipa_client_config` o `realm_join` — reproducible.

## Autorización
- `root` para join realm + config SSSD
- AD admin credentials para initial join (o pre-created computer object)
- Users authenticated via AD credentials (no local passwords)

title: Linux: Samba + NFS shares para file sharing
excerpt: Share files entre Linux, Windows, Mac con Samba y NFS.
body:
## Samba (SMB/CIFS)
Interoperability con Windows shares.

### Install
**RHEL**:
```bash
sudo dnf install samba samba-client
```

**Ubuntu**:
```bash
sudo apt install samba smbclient
```

### Basic config `/etc/samba/smb.conf`
```ini
[global]
    workgroup = EMPRESA
    server string = File Server
    security = user
    map to guest = bad user
    log file = /var/log/samba/log.%m
    max log size = 1000
    dns proxy = no
    server min protocol = SMB2

[shared]
    path = /srv/samba/shared
    browsable = yes
    writable = yes
    guest ok = no
    valid users = @sambausers
    create mask = 0664
    directory mask = 0775

[public]
    path = /srv/samba/public
    browsable = yes
    writable = yes
    guest ok = yes
    guest only = yes

[secure]
    path = /srv/samba/secure
    browsable = no
    writable = yes
    valid users = alice, bob, @finance
    force group = finance
    create mask = 0660
    directory mask = 0770
```

### Test config
```bash
sudo testparm
```

### Create paths
```bash
sudo mkdir -p /srv/samba/{shared,public,secure}
sudo chown -R nobody:nobody /srv/samba/public
sudo chmod -R 777 /srv/samba/public
sudo chown -R root:sambausers /srv/samba/shared
sudo chmod -R 2775 /srv/samba/shared    # setgid — new files inherit group
sudo chown -R root:finance /srv/samba/secure
sudo chmod -R 2770 /srv/samba/secure
```

### Create Samba users
Samba maintains separate password DB:
```bash
sudo useradd -M -s /sbin/nologin alice     # Linux user (no login)
sudo smbpasswd -a alice                     # add to Samba DB
sudo smbpasswd -e alice                     # enable
```

### Start
```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now smb nmb          # RHEL
sudo systemctl enable --now smbd nmbd        # Ubuntu
```

### Firewall
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=samba --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
```

### SELinux (RHEL)
```bash
sudo setsebool -P samba_enable_home_dirs on
sudo setsebool -P samba_export_all_rw on    # careful — allow all shares
sudo semanage fcontext -a -t samba_share_t '/srv/samba(/.*)?'
sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/samba
```

### Test
From Linux client:
```bash
smbclient -L //server-ip -U alice
smbclient //server-ip/shared -U alice
# smb: \> ls
# smb: \> get file.txt
```

From Windows: `\\server-ip\shared`.

### Mount permanent
```bash
sudo mkdir /mnt/shared
sudo mount -t cifs //server-ip/shared /mnt/shared -o username=alice,password=xxx,uid=1000,gid=1000

# Permanent en /etc/fstab
//server-ip/shared  /mnt/shared  cifs  credentials=/root/.smbcredentials,uid=1000,gid=1000  0  0
```

`/root/.smbcredentials` (chmod 600):
```
username=alice
password=xxx
```

## AD integration (Samba member server)
Samba en Linux joined a AD domain:

### Config `/etc/samba/smb.conf`
```ini
[global]
    workgroup = EMPRESA
    security = ADS
    realm = EMPRESA.LOCAL
    kerberos method = system keytab
    template shell = /bin/bash
    winbind use default domain = yes
    winbind offline logon = false
    winbind refresh tickets = yes
    winbind enum users = no
    winbind enum groups = no

    idmap config * : backend = tdb
    idmap config * : range = 3000-7999
    idmap config EMPRESA : backend = rid
    idmap config EMPRESA : range = 10000-999999
```

### Join domain
```bash
sudo net ads join -U admin@EMPRESA.LOCAL
```

### Enable winbind
```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now winbind
```

### Verify
```bash
sudo wbinfo -u          # AD users
sudo wbinfo -g          # AD groups
id alice@empresa.local
```

### Share con AD users
```ini
[dept]
    path = /srv/samba/dept
    writable = yes
    valid users = @'EMPRESA\department_users'
```

## NFS (Network File System)
Unix/Linux native file sharing.

### Install (server)
**RHEL**:
```bash
sudo dnf install nfs-utils
```

**Ubuntu**:
```bash
sudo apt install nfs-kernel-server
```

### Export `/etc/exports`
```
/srv/nfs/shared     10.0.0.0/8(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,no_root_squash)
/srv/nfs/public     *(ro,sync,no_subtree_check,all_squash)
/srv/nfs/homes      10.0.0.0/8(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,root_squash)
```

### Opciones
- **rw** / **ro** — read-write / read-only
- **sync** — writes sync antes de respond (safer)
- **async** — respond antes de disk commit (faster, risky)
- **no_subtree_check** — reduce overhead
- **root_squash** — remote root → nfsnobody (default, safer)
- **no_root_squash** — remote root can operate as local root (dangerous)
- **all_squash** — todos users → nfsnobody
- **anonuid=1000,anongid=1000** — squash to specific uid/gid
- **secure** — require ports <1024 (default)
- **insecure** — allow high ports

### Apply
```bash
sudo exportfs -ra
sudo systemctl enable --now nfs-server
```

Ubuntu service:
```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now nfs-kernel-server
```

### Firewall
```bash
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=nfs --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=rpc-bind --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=mountd --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
```

### Ver exports actuales
```bash
sudo exportfs -v
showmount -e localhost
```

### Mount desde cliente
```bash
sudo dnf install nfs-utils           # RHEL
sudo apt install nfs-common          # Ubuntu

sudo mkdir /mnt/nfs
sudo mount -t nfs4 server-ip:/srv/nfs/shared /mnt/nfs
```

### Permanent `/etc/fstab`
```
server-ip:/srv/nfs/shared  /mnt/nfs  nfs4  rw,noatime,_netdev  0  0
```

`_netdev` = wait for network before mount.

### NFSv3 vs NFSv4
**NFSv3** (legacy):
- Multiple ports (statd, mountd, lockd) — firewall tricky
- No encryption
- Old auth (AUTH_SYS)

**NFSv4** (modern):
- Single port (2049)
- Better perf
- Kerberos auth support (sec=krb5)
- Pseudo-filesystem (fsid=0)
- Better locking

Use `-t nfs4` para explicit v4.

### NFSv4 Kerberos auth
```
/srv/nfs/secure  10.0.0.0/8(rw,sec=krb5p,sync)
```

- `krb5` — auth only
- `krb5i` — auth + integrity (checksums)
- `krb5p` — auth + integrity + privacy (encryption)

Requires Kerberos setup en client + server.

## Samba vs NFS
| Feature | Samba (SMB) | NFS |
|---------|-------------|-----|
| Native OS | Windows | Unix/Linux |
| Cross-platform | Excellent | Linux-focused |
| Auth | User/pass, AD, Kerberos | Unix uid/gid, Kerberos |
| Encryption | SMB3 encryption | NFSv4 with krb5p |
| Perf | Good | Excellent (LAN) |
| Complex ACLs | Yes | Basic (NFS4 ACL en v4) |

### Cuándo cada uno
- **Windows clients** → Samba
- **Mixed environments** → Samba (Mac + Linux + Windows)
- **Linux-only LAN** → NFS (better perf)
- **AD integration** → Samba con winbind
- **Kerberos required** → NFSv4 con krb5p

## Performance tuning

### Samba
```ini
[global]
    socket options = TCP_NODELAY IPTOS_LOWDELAY
    read raw = yes
    write raw = yes
    max xmit = 65535
    dead time = 15
    getwd cache = yes
```

### NFS mount options
```
sync,rsize=1048576,wsize=1048576,noatime,nodiratime
```

- `rsize/wsize` — I/O block size (larger = fewer round trips)
- `noatime/nodiratime` — reduce metadata updates

## Common issues

### 'Cannot access Samba share'
- Firewall blocking ports 137, 138, 139, 445
- SELinux `samba_share_t` context missing
- User not en `smbpasswd`
- Wrong password
- File permissions restrictive

### 'NFS mount hangs'
- Server unreachable (network issue)
- Firewall blocking
- Wrong export path
- Mount option `soft` para timeout (default `hard` = wait forever)

### 'Files owned por nobody'
- User ID mismatch: client uid 1001 ≠ server uid 1001
- Solution: NFSv4 con idmapd, o synchronize uids across systems

### 'Cannot write to NFS share'
- Server export `ro`
- Root squash converting root → nfsnobody
- File permissions restrictive on server
- SELinux blocking

### 'Samba show performance drop'
- SMB1 disabled (default en modern) — old clients need SMB2/3
- Network issues (ping tests, iperf)
- Antivirus scanning en server side

## Best practices

### 1. Use SMB3 encryption
```ini
[shared]
    smb encrypt = required
```

Encrypts data in-transit.

### 2. Use NFSv4 con krb5p
Encrypts NFS traffic. Requires setup effort.

### 3. Firewall
Restrict shares a specific networks/subnets.

### 4. Backup exclusions
Some files don't backup well (open, locks). Documenta.

### 5. Monitoring
- Samba: `smbstatus` — active connections
- NFS: `nfsstat` — server statistics

### 6. Quotas
For Linux users: `edquota` (ext4/XFS). Limit per user en share.

### 7. Snapshots
Use ZFS or LVM snapshots underlying share. Fast recovery from deletion.

### 8. Access logs
Audit access — SIEM integration.

### 9. Documentation
List of shares, users allowed, purpose, backup policy.

## Autorización
- `root` para config server + create exports
- Samba: `smbpasswd` para user password DB
- NFS: uid-based auth (or Kerberos)

title: Linux: monitoring — disk, memory, IO, network
tags: monitoring, sar, iostat, vmstat, top, htop, linux
excerpt: Herramientas core para monitor performance Linux.
body:
## Real-time overview

### top
Standard. Runs con `top`, quit con `q`.

#### Interactive keys
- `1` — per-CPU breakdown
- `M` — sort by memory
- `P` — sort by CPU (default)
- `T` — sort by cumulative time
- `u` — filter por user
- `k` — kill process
- `r` — renice
- `c` — full command line

### htop
Mejor UI. Install: `sudo dnf install htop` o `apt install htop`.
- Color-coded
- Mouse support
- Tree view (`F5`)
- Filter (`F4`)

### atop
Combines top con system stats — CPU, memory, disk, network en one view.
```bash
sudo dnf install atop
```

Records historical: `atop -r /var/log/atop/atop_YYYYMMDD`.

## CPU

### mpstat
```bash
mpstat 5       # every 5 sec
mpstat -P ALL 5   # per CPU
```

### uptime
```bash
uptime
# 15:32:10 up 45 days,  8:23,  3 users,  load average: 0.42, 0.58, 0.71
```

**Load average**: procesos en run queue durante 1, 5, 15 min. Rough rule: <(cores × 0.7) es healthy.

### `/proc/loadavg`
```bash
cat /proc/loadavg
# 0.42 0.58 0.71 3/512 12345
#                 |    |
#       running/total  last-pid
```

### CPU info
```bash
lscpu
cat /proc/cpuinfo
nproc          # count of processors
```

## Memory

### free
```bash
free -h
#                 total   used   free   shared   buff/cache   available
# Mem:            15Gi    2.1Gi  8.5Gi  100Mi    4.8Gi        12Gi
# Swap:           4.0Gi   0B     4.0Gi
```

**Available** = the important number (usable free + reclaimable cache).

### vmstat
```bash
vmstat 5
# procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
#  r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
#  1  0      0 8912344 234512 5089432    0    0    23    89  345  678  5  2 92  1  0
```

**Columns críticas**:
- `r` — processes en run queue (>cores = CPU bottleneck)
- `b` — blocked (waiting I/O)
- `si/so` — swap in/out (any = memory pressure)
- `bi/bo` — block in/out (disk I/O)
- `us/sy/id/wa` — CPU % (user/system/idle/iowait)
- `wa` >20% = I/O bottleneck

### /proc/meminfo
```bash
cat /proc/meminfo
```

Detailed breakdown.

### Kill by memory
```bash
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head
# Or via top: M luego k luego PID
```

### OOM killer
Events:
```bash
dmesg | grep -i 'killed process'
journalctl -k | grep -i oom
```

Kernel kills highest-memory process al OOM (out-of-memory).

### Swappiness
```bash
cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness
# 60 default — how aggressive swap out
```

DBs typically set 10 (menos swap).

## Disk I/O

### iostat
```bash
sudo dnf install sysstat        # if not installed
iostat -x 5      # extended stats every 5s
```

Output:
```
Device   r/s   w/s   rMB/s   wMB/s   r_await   w_await   %util
sda      12.3  45.7  0.5     2.1     3.2       8.4       78.5
```

**Métricas críticas**:
- `%util` >80% = disk bottleneck
- `r_await/w_await` >20ms = slow storage
- `r/s + w/s` — IOPS

### iotop
Like top pero para I/O:
```bash
sudo dnf install iotop
sudo iotop -o    # only processes doing I/O
```

Muestra which processes están I/O-bound.

### df
```bash
df -h            # human-readable
df -hT           # con filesystem type
df -i            # inodes (files count vs available)
```

### du
```bash
du -sh /var/log      # summary size
du -sh /var/*        # per subdirectory
du -sh /var/* | sort -rh | head       # top consumers
```

### ncdu
Interactive du:
```bash
sudo dnf install ncdu
ncdu /
```

Navigable UI para find large directories.

## Network

### ss (moderno)
Reemplaza netstat:
```bash
ss -tuln         # listening TCP + UDP
ss -tunap        # con processes
ss -s            # summary stats
ss -tn           # established TCP
```

### netstat (legacy)
```bash
netstat -tuln    # listening
netstat -antp    # con processes
```

### iftop
Real-time network throughput per connection:
```bash
sudo dnf install iftop
sudo iftop -i eth0
```

### nethogs
Per-process network usage:
```bash
sudo dnf install nethogs
sudo nethogs eth0
```

### iperf
Bandwidth testing:
```bash
# On server
iperf3 -s

# On client
iperf3 -c server-ip
```

### ping / traceroute
Basic connectivity:
```bash
ping -c 5 host.empresa.local
traceroute host.empresa.local
mtr host.empresa.local          # combined ping + traceroute
```

## sar (historical + long-term)
Part of sysstat package. Recording system activity durante time.

### Enable
```bash
sudo systemctl enable --now sysstat
```

Collects every 10 min → `/var/log/sa/` files.

### View
```bash
sar                    # today's CPU (default)
sar -u                 # CPU
sar -r                 # memory
sar -b                 # I/O
sar -n DEV             # network per interface
sar -q                 # queue length + load
sar -W                 # swap activity

# Historical
sar -f /var/log/sa/sa15     # data from 15th of month
sar -s 09:00:00 -e 12:00:00 # solo 9-12 window
```

### KSar
Java GUI para plot sar data. https://sourceforge.net/projects/ksar/

## Custom monitoring

### sysstat cron
`/etc/cron.d/sysstat` — collects every 10 min:
```
*/10 * * * * root /usr/lib64/sa/sa1 1 1
53 23 * * * root /usr/lib64/sa/sa2 -A
```

### Bash script alerts
```bash
#!/bin/bash
# alert-disk-full.sh
for mp in $(df -h --output=target,pcent | tail -n +2 | awk '$2+0 > 90 {print $1}'); do
    echo "DISK ALERT: $mp is >90% full" | mail -s 'Disk Alert' admin@empresa.com
done
```

Schedule con cron:
```
0 * * * * /usr/local/bin/alert-disk-full.sh
```

### CPU load alert
```bash
load=$(uptime | awk -F'load average:' '{print $2}' | awk '{print $1}' | tr -d ',')
if (( $(echo "$load > 5.0" | bc -l) )); then
    echo "High load: $load" | mail admin@empresa.com
fi
```

## Advanced tools

### perf
Kernel-level profiling:
```bash
sudo dnf install perf
sudo perf top             # real-time hot functions
sudo perf record -a -g sleep 10
sudo perf report          # analyze recording
```

### strace
Syscall tracing:
```bash
strace -p <PID>           # attach a process
strace -e open ls         # solo open calls
strace -c ls              # count calls (summary)
```

Útil para debugging 'why is this slow'.

### tcpdump
Network capture:
```bash
sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w capture.pcap port 80
sudo tcpdump -i any host 10.0.0.5
```

Read con Wireshark.

### lsof
Open files + connections:
```bash
sudo lsof -i :80          # what's using port 80
sudo lsof -p <PID>        # files opened por process
sudo lsof /var/log        # what's accessing directory
sudo lsof -u alice        # files opened por user
```

### fuser
```bash
sudo fuser -mv /mnt/nfs      # processes using mount
sudo fuser -kv /mnt/nfs      # kill those processes
```

## Enterprise monitoring stacks

### Prometheus + Grafana
Métricas + dashboards + alerts.

Exporters:
- `node_exporter` — Linux metrics
- `blackbox_exporter` — endpoints probing
- `mysqld_exporter`, `postgres_exporter`, etc.

### Zabbix
Agent-based, mature.

### Datadog / New Relic / Dynatrace
Cloud SaaS con Linux agents.

### ELK / OpenSearch
Logs. `filebeat` agent.

### Netdata
Install en 1 line, extensive dashboards:
```bash
bash <(curl -Ss https://my-netdata.io/kickstart.sh)
```

## Common issues

### 'Server slow — no obvious cause'
1. `top` — high CPU?
2. `free -h` — memory pressure?
3. `iostat -x 5` — disk %util?
4. `vmstat 5` — wa >20% (I/O wait)?
5. `dmesg | tail` — hardware errors?
6. `journalctl --since '1 hour ago' | grep -i error`

### 'Memory leak'
- `ps aux --sort=-%mem` — top consumers
- Track over time (sar -r)
- Restart offending process
- Root cause en app code

### 'High load pero CPU idle'
Usually I/O wait. `iostat -x`, `iotop`.

### 'Disk full pero du shows less'
- Deleted files still open: `sudo lsof +L1`
- Kill process holding: reclaims space

## Best practices

### 1. Baseline first
Record 1 week normal ops. Any deviation = investigate.

### 2. Monitor everything
CPU, memory, disk (per volume), network (per interface), disk I/O, load avg.

### 3. Alerts thresholds razonables
- CPU >85% sustained 10 min
- Memory available <10%
- Disk >90%
- Load >(cores × 2)

### 4. Log a SIEM
Retain historical trends.

### 5. Trending
Grafana dashboards con 30-day retention minimum.

### 6. Alerting fatigue
Not everything an alert. Warnings vs pages.

### 7. Runbooks per alert
What to check, escalation path.

## Autorización
- Most tools no require root para read
- Some (iotop, tcpdump, perf, sar historical) require root
- Sudo delegation via /etc/sudoers.d/

title: AIX: HACMP / PowerHA cluster para HA
excerpt: PowerHA (HACMP) — HA clustering para AIX critical workloads.
body:
## PowerHA SystemMirror
IBM HA clustering solution para AIX (antes HACMP). Provides:
- Auto failover de resources
- Shared storage entre nodes
- IP takeover
- Application monitoring
- Rolling upgrades

### Use cases
- SAP HANA on AIX (rare pero exists)
- Oracle DB on AIX
- Critical apps requiring 99.99% uptime

## Terminology

### Cluster
Set of nodes acting como one HA unit.

### Node
AIX LPAR participating en cluster.

### Resource Group (RG)
Collection de resources (IP, VG, app) que failover together.

### Application Server
Scripts para start/stop application.

### Service IP
Virtual IP that clients use. Follows the active node.

### Shared VG
Volume Group visible a all cluster nodes (via SAN).

### Non-Concurrent Access
One node owns VG at a time (typical).

### Concurrent Access
Multiple nodes read/write simultaneously (Oracle RAC).

## Requirements

### Hardware
- 2+ Power servers
- Shared storage (SAN — NPIV vSCSI para VIOS setup)
- Redundant networks (multiple adapters)
- Serial heartbeat (opcional pero recomendado)

### Software
- AIX 7.2 TL4+ o AIX 7.3
- PowerHA 7.2.x licensed
- All nodes: identical AIX + PowerHA versions

### Network
- **Service networks** — where clients connect
- **Boot IPs** — permanent per-node IPs
- **Persistent IPs** — administrative
- **Heartbeat networks** — cluster comms (isolated)

## Install

### On each node
```bash
smit install_all      # install PowerHA filesets
# Or:
installp -aXY -d /path/to/media all
```

Required filesets:
- `cluster.es.server.*`
- `cluster.es.client.*`
- `cluster.es.smui.*`

### Verify
```bash
lslpp -l cluster.*
```

## Cluster setup

### CAA (Cluster Aware AIX)
Underlying framework — PowerHA sits on top.

```bash
# Create cluster
mkcluster -n mycluster -m node1,node2 -d hdisk10   # hdisk10 = repository disk (small shared)

# Verify
lscluster -m
lscluster -s
```

### PowerHA config

### 1. SMIT
```bash
smit sysmirror
```

Menu:
- Custom Cluster Configuration
- Standard Cluster Configuration (guided)

### 2. clmgr (CLI)
```bash
# Add cluster
clmgr add cluster mycluster NODES=node1,node2

# Add repository disk
clmgr modify cluster mycluster REPOSITORY=hdisk10

# Add resource group
clmgr add rg RG_APP1 NODES=node1,node2 STARTUP=OHN FALLBACK=NFB

# Add service IP
clmgr add service_ip service_ip1 NETWORK=net_ether_01 IPADDR=10.0.0.100

# Add shared VG
clmgr add vg shared_vg1 PHYSICAL_VOLUMES=hdisk11,hdisk12 RG=RG_APP1

# Add application server
clmgr add app_ctrl app1 STARTSCRIPT=/usr/local/scripts/start_app.sh STOPSCRIPT=/usr/local/scripts/stop_app.sh

# Attach app a RG
clmgr modify rg RG_APP1 APPLICATIONS=app1 SERVICE_LABEL=service_ip1 VOLUME_GROUP=shared_vg1
```

### 3. Verify + sync
```bash
clmgr verify cluster
clmgr sync cluster
```

All changes propagated a all nodes.

### 4. Start
```bash
clmgr start cluster

# Ver estado
clmgr view cluster mycluster
clRGinfo                       # resource group info
clmgr query rg
```

## Application scripts

### /usr/local/scripts/start_app.sh
```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Start SAP or Oracle
su - orasid -c 'lsnrctl start && sqlplus / as sysdba <<EOF
startup;
exit
EOF'

if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
    exit 0
else
    exit 1
fi
```

### /usr/local/scripts/stop_app.sh
```bash
#!/bin/bash
su - orasid -c 'sqlplus / as sysdba <<EOF
shutdown immediate;
exit
EOF
lsnrctl stop'
exit $?
```

### Ownership
```bash
chmod +x /usr/local/scripts/*.sh
chown root:system /usr/local/scripts/*.sh
```

Must be identical on both nodes.

## Failover types

### Startup Policies
- **OHN** (Online on Home Node) — start solo en home node
- **OFAN** (Online on First Available Node) — first up
- **OAAN** (Online on All Available Nodes) — concurrent
- **OUDP** (Online Using Distribution Policy) — spread

### Fallover Policies
- **FNPN** (Fallover to Next Priority Node)
- **FUDNP** (Fallover Using Dynamic Node Priority)
- **BONN** (Bring Offline on Next Available Node)

### Fallback Policies
- **NFB** (Never Fallback) — stay en target hasta manual
- **FBHPN** (Fallback to Higher Priority Node) — auto return

## Test failover

### Manual
```bash
# Stop cluster services en node1 (RG moves to node2)
clmgr stop node node1 WHEN=now MANAGE=takeover

# Verify
clRGinfo         # RG_APP1 should be en node2

# Restart node1
clmgr start node node1
```

### Verify app works desde node2
- Ping service IP: reaches node2
- Connect to app: functional
- No data loss

## Storage details

### Shared VG
- Created **manually first** en one node
- Then use PowerHA to add al cluster (avoids concurrent access)

```bash
# On node1
mkvg -y shared_vg1 -s 128 hdisk11 hdisk12
varyoffvg shared_vg1

# On node2
importvg -y shared_vg1 hdisk11
varyoffvg shared_vg1

# Now add to PowerHA:
clmgr add vg shared_vg1 RG=RG_APP1 PHYSICAL_VOLUMES=hdisk11,hdisk12
```

### VG major numbers
Must be same across all nodes:
```bash
lsvg -m shared_vg1
```

If different, sync using `chdev`.

## Monitoring

### Command line
```bash
clRGinfo -m        # resource group with node details
clmgr view cluster
clmgr query cluster
cllsclstr          # legacy

# Node status
clmgr query node -type ALL

# Recent errors
lssrc -a | grep -i cluster
errpt -j <cluster-error-id>
```

### SMUI (SystemMirror UI)
Web UI (moderno). Provides:
- Dashboard
- Historical events
- Health checks
- Actionable alerts

```bash
https://mycluster-mgmt.empresa.local
```

### Logs
- `/var/hacmp/log/` — PowerHA logs
- `/var/hacmp/log/hacmp.out` — main log
- `/var/hacmp/log/cluster.log` — recent events
- `/tmp/clstrmgr.debug` — startup issues

Review `hacmp.out` durante troubleshooting.

## Common issues

### 'Node cannot join cluster'
- Repository disk not accessible
- Time skew (need NTP)
- Firewall blocking cluster ports
- SSH keys not synced

### 'RG stuck en Error state'
- Verify shared VG accessible
- Start/stop script errors — check `hacmp.out`
- Manual online after fix:
```bash
clRGmove -g RG_APP1 -n node1
```

### 'Split brain'
Both nodes think they own resources — network partition.

Repository disk (with fencing) should prevent.

### 'App fails to start after failover'
- Prerequisites not met en target node (missing files, wrong perms)
- Sync app config (`rsync`) between nodes
- Test manual start on each node

### 'Slow failover'
- App shutdown script hangs
- File system unmount slow
- IP takeover slow
- Tune application scripts (add timeouts)

### 'False failover trigger'
- Heartbeat network flaky
- Add redundant networks
- Increase heartbeat intervals (careful — real failures detected slower)

## Rolling upgrades
Upgrade PowerHA sin downtime:

1. Move RGs off node1 (all to node2)
2. Upgrade PowerHA en node1
3. Reboot node1
4. Verify
5. Move RGs back a node1
6. Repeat para node2

Steps:
```bash
clmgr stop node node1 MANAGE=move
# Upgrade node1
clmgr start node node1
clmgr move rg RG_APP1 NODE=node1
```

## Best practices

### 1. Test failover regularmente
Every 3 months minimum. Practice = confidence.

### 2. Application scripts idempotent
Safe to run multiple times. Handle edge cases.

### 3. Timeout limits
App start/stop scripts should timeout gracefully.

### 4. Monitoring integration
Alert on RG state changes, offline resources, cluster errors.

### 5. Documentation
- Cluster topology diagram
- Node roles + priorities
- Application dependencies
- Contact list (DBA, app owners)
- Escalation matrix

### 6. Backup config
```bash
snapclient --create /backup/cluster-config-$(date +%F).tar.gz
```

Before/after major changes.

### 7. NTP mandatory
All nodes time-synced.

### 8. Redundant networks
At least 2 heartbeat networks. Different switches/paths.

### 9. Repository disk
Small shared disk (1 GB). Isolated from data disks. Persistent SCSI reservation.

### 10. Verify after changes
```bash
clmgr verify cluster -type Automatic
```

Before syncing.

## Autorización
- `root` para cluster admin
- SMUI RBAC roles: Administrator, Operator, Viewer

## Migration to Linux (trend)
Muchos SAP on AIX/PowerHA migrando a Linux/Pacemaker. Same concepts, diferentes tools:
- Pacemaker + Corosync (Linux HA)
- SUSE HAE / RHEL HA Add-On

Skills transferable — planning + testing + monitoring.
